problem: Image-as-node topological maps lack object-level reasoning and connectivity, while 3D metric maps and 3D scene graphs need precise geometry and heavy computation. Prior segment or pixel-level approaches are not open-vocabulary queryable or purely topological.
motivation: Robots need maps that support open-vocabulary object-goal navigation without a learned, embodiment-specific policy or 3D reconstruction. Foundation models (SAM, CLIP, DINO/DINOv2) now make segment-level, semantically meaningful and persistent landmarks feasible as graph nodes.
key_idea: Build a purely topological graph whose nodes are SAM image segments, linked across consecutive images by descriptor matching and within an image by Delaunay triangulation over centroids, then plan Dijkstra 'hops' over segment tracks and servo toward them.
insight: Inter-image edge weight 0 versus intra-image weight 1 makes shortest paths prefer persistent segment tracks, which yields sub-goals a simple controller can follow. Graph-convolution neighbor aggregation of descriptors adds 'place' context; in the GPCampus ablation (Fig. 5), Recall@1 for DINO and DINOv2 improves with more GC layers and with adding inter-image edges. DINO beats CLIP for segment instance and category association (Table I), so CLIP is used only for language querying.
method: Segment nodes: SAM segments per image, each with a centroid, binary mask and l2-normalized DINO/DINOv2 descriptor from pooled pixel features. CLIP is used to drop 'stuff' segments (floor, ceiling, wall).

Edges: intra-image edges from Delaunay triangulation of centroids; inter-image edges by nearest-neighbor descriptor match within a 1-3 frame window, kept if similarity exceeds θ, with a fallback edge so the graph stays connected. No loop closures.

Descriptor aggregation: simplified GCN, H(l+1)=D̃^-1 Ã H(l), with lmax=2, applied to both map and query image to add neighborhood context. Localization is segment-level retrieval by thresholded similarity.
Planning: Dijkstra with weight 0 for inter-image edges and 1 for intra-image edges. Two variants: Intra-DT (Delaunay edges, smoother) and Intra-All (full subgraph per image, allows long hops).

Navigation: Discrete mode matches each plan node in the current view, with lost/track/hop states from pixel offset and segment size ratio, driven by a PID controller. Continuous mode computes a path-length-weighted average of horizontal offsets over matched submap segments.
Open-vocabulary relational query: GPT-4 parses the query into reference and target text. CLIP retrieves the top-3 nodes for each, and Dijkstra picks the target-reference pair with the shortest path.

setting.backbone: SAM + DINO/DINOv2 + CLIP (frozen foundation models) + GPT-4 (frozen, for query parsing); PID controller
setting.observation: monocular RGB image sequence (perspective crops from panoramas in some experiments)
setting.action_space: continuous yaw velocity from PID on pixel offset, with small fixed forward velocity
setting.simulator: Habitat (skokloster scene) for navigation demo; Gibson and GPCampus/PanoContext data for offline evaluation; real robot trials
setting.privileged: none (GT segments/instances used only for the Gibson data-association evaluation, not for navigation)

numbers.eval_set_note: House Klickitat only; 544 SAM-segment views of 68 objects from 18 categories, GT instance assignment via IoU≥0.2
numbers.method: RoboHop segment association with DINO descriptors
numbers.extra: nearest-neighbor top-1 matching; CLIP comparison row: instance 35.11, category 62.87
numbers.evidence: Table I: Accuracy of segment-level object recognition (DINO 56.43% / 79.04%)

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark results; navigation is qualitative and preliminary. GPCampus localization results (Recall@1 vs GC layers) are only shown in Fig. 5, with no numbers in the text.
results: DINO segment descriptors beat CLIP for segment-level association (56.43% vs 35.11% instance, 79.04% vs 62.87% category). Localization Recall@1 on GPCampus rises with more graph-convolution layers and with more inter-image edges. Qualitative plans and preliminary zero-shot navigation in Habitat and the real world show segment-hopping works without a learned policy.
limitations: Depends heavily on segment association quality; repetitive or aliased structures (paintings, chairs) cause mismatches, and LightGlue worked better than DINOv2 there.
Cannot handle dynamic environments; 'stuff' segments (carpet, ground) can persist, and segmentation is not repeatable across revisits, which corrupts the size ratio used for hop and forward motion.
Evaluation is qualitative and preliminary, with no standard benchmark; relational queries via LLM lack metric information for 'next to' reasoning.
